title: Effect of Annealing on Maze Domains in Topological Insulator - Magnetic Multilayer Heterostructures
authors: Benjamin A. Brereton, Soumyarup Hait, Christy J. Kinane, Francesco Maccherozzi, Ahmet Yagmur, Satoshi Sasaki, Thomas A. Moore, Sean Langridge, Christopher H. Marrows
abstract: Combining topological insulators with chiral magnetic multilayers offers the opportunity to greatly enhance the spin-orbit torque (SOT) driven manipulation of hosted spin textures, however this also exposes devices to the often poor temperature stability of the commonly used, Bi$_2$X$_3$-based (X is a chalcogenic element), topological insulator films. In this work we demonstrate through in-situ-annealing and polarised neutron reflectometry that the multilayer at a Bi$_2$Se$_3$ interface remains magnetically robust up to a temperature of 350 $^{\circ}$C: even as the Bi$_2$Se$_3$ epilayer structurally deteriorates. Through x-ray photoemission electron microscopy, an intermediate annealing temperature of $\sim$ 200 $^{\circ}$C was found to improve the domain ordering of the multilayer, allowing for field-induced skyrmion nucleation, all whilst sustaining minimal damage to the topological insulator
summary: This work demonstrates that optimizing the annealing temperature is crucial for maintaining the functionality of Topological Insulator/Magnetic Multilayer heterostructures. By using advanced techniques like PNR and XRD, the authors pinpoint an optimal annealing window ($\sim 200^\circ	ext{C}$) that enhances magnetic domain ordering and stabilizes skyrmions without causing detrimental structural damage to the underlying TI film.
main_problem: The study investigates how annealing temperature affects the magnetic domain ordering and structural integrity of Topological Insulator - Magnetic Multilayer Heterostructures.
main_result: Annealing at an intermediate temperature ($\sim 200^\circ	ext{C}$) optimizes magnetic domain ordering, enabling skyrmion nucleation, while high temperatures ($350^\circ	ext{C}$) cause significant structural deterioration of the TI film.
method: The research employs a combination of *in-situ* annealing, Polarized Neutron Reflectometry (PNR) for depth-resolved magnetism, X-ray Diffraction (XRD) for crystallinity, and Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) for surface topography.
model_or_system: The physical system is a multilayer heterostructure combining a Topological Insulator ($	ext{Bi}_2	ext{Se}_3$) with chiral magnetic multilayers (e.g., $	ext{Pt}/	ext{CoB}/	ext{Ru}$). The analysis models the magnetic response using slab fitting techniques.
key_observables: Spin Asymmetry ($	ext{SA}$), saturation magnetization ($	ext{M}_s$), effective anisotropy field ($	ext{H}_k$), domain width, and XRD peak intensities/shifts.
important_parameters: Annealing temperatures ($200^\circ	ext{C}$ vs $350^\circ	ext{C}$), magnetic field range ($\pm 2 	ext{ T}$), and the structural loss percentage of Selenium ($	ext{Se}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that changes in reflectivity are primarily magnetic in origin when fitting PNR data, and that structural degradation (Se loss) can be modeled using site-specific vacancy calculations.
figures_summary: Figures compare magnetic hysteresis loops and structural data (XRR/XRD) before and after annealing at different temperatures, showing the optimal balance between magnetic enhancement and structural preservation.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the magnetic and structural properties across a temperature gradient, using PNR and XRD to diagnose the physical mechanisms behind changes in magnetic ordering (domain size) versus material degradation (crystallinity loss).
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the precise control over interfacial properties via thermal annealing and the study of emergent topological magnetic textures (skyrmions) are highly relevant to developing quantum spintronic devices.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Sample structure and magnetic characterisation. (a) Schematic of sample including an impression of the effect of TI terracing. Here the relative scale of the terrace heights has been exaggerated for clarity; (b) SQUID VSM M(H) hysteresis loops measured at room temperature in in-plane and out of plane geometries for as grown and 350 ◦C annealed samples. The magnetic moment/area value extracted from PNR slab model fittings in Fig. 3(b) is additionally shown as the large markers. Inset axes show normalised in-plane curves for both temperatures.

Figure 2. Structural changes to samples due to annealing. (a) XRR curves taken after annealing at different temperatures. The Bi2Se3(003) XRD peak is marked. The curves are vertically offset for clarity; (b-c) 2 µm × 2 µm atomic force microscopy images of samples (b) as grown and (c) after 350 ◦C annealing.

Figure 3. Polarised neutron reflectometry measurements after successive annealing steps at increasing temperature: (a) shows the spin asymmetry profiles for as-grown (20 ◦C ) and after a 350 ◦C anneal, including their respective fits corresponding to slab models for which the SLD profiles are shown in (b). Respective 2σ confidence ranges are shown. Shown in (c) are the intermediate temperature measurements with either 20 or 350 ◦C fits overlaid where they best describe the data.

Figure 4. The effect of annealing on the observed domain structure: X-PEEM images on samples (a) before and (b) after a 200 ◦C anneal. The included scale bar in (a) represents 5 µm for both (a) and (b). In (b) skyrmion-like features are highlighted by yellow circles. (c-f) shows field evolution of the highlighted region in (b) under an increasing applied field resulting in isolated skyrmion nucleation; (g) shows the radial FFT intensity dependence for both (a) and (b) with fitted log-normal distributions.
